title: History
intro: From Carême and Escoffier to the Creole cookbooks of nineteenth century New Orleans, the people and books that shaped this cooking. The dates and the sources travel with every claim.

entries.title: La Varenne
entries.summary: François Pierre de La Varenne, cook to the Marquis d'Uxelles, published Le Cuisinier françois in 1651. It traded heavy spice for the taste of the food itself and set down bouillon, roux and reduction as working tools.
entries.guest: La Varenne was a seventeenth-century French cook whose book of 1651 helped turn French cooking towards butter, herbs and the true taste of the food.

paras: François Pierre, known as La Varenne, was a French cook of the seventeenth century, born around 1615 (sources differ by a few years), who died in 1678. He ran the kitchen of Louis Chalon du Blé, Marquis d'Uxelles, governor of Chalon-sur-Saône, and in 1651 he published Le Cuisinier françois, The French Cook, in Paris. It was reprinted again and again and reached English readers in 1653.

It matters to a cook today because so much of the daily work at the stove is already in it in an early form: a sauce built on stock, thickened with flour cooked in fat, reduced until it tastes of itself and finished with butter and herbs.

The book rests on a few tools still on your station. The first is the bouillon, a broth of meat, bones and vegetables simmered long, kept ready and used to cook and moisten almost everything else. The second is reduction: simmering a liquid uncovered so water steams away and flavour concentrates. Reduce 1 litre (about 1 quart) of stock by half and you have 500 ml (about 2 cups) that tastes deeper and has more body; it coats a spoon only when reduced much further, towards a glaze. Season after reducing, never before, because the salt concentrates too.

The third is a binder: a liaison of flour browned in melted lard, kept ready to stir into sauces, among the earliest printed forms of what cooks soon called roux. Making one today belongs to its own entry. The fourth is a bundle of herbs tied together to flavour a pot and come out whole, the ancestor of the bouquet garni: today parsley stalks, thyme and bay tied with string.

The fifth is the mushroom hash cooks call duxelles. Chop 450 g (1 lb) of mushrooms and 60 g (2 oz) of shallot very fine. Soften the shallot in 30 g (1 oz) of butter over medium heat for 2 minutes, add the mushrooms and cook, stirring, for 10 to 15 minutes, until their water has steamed away and the pan sizzles rather than bubbles. Season, add parsley and cool it on a tray. It fills a beef Wellington and stuffs mushrooms.

What descends from the book is a way of cooking more than a list of dishes. Its stock-based sauces lead, by way of Carême, to the sauce families a classical kitchen still teaches. Its liaison of fat and flour is an early printed ancestor of the roux, from the white roux of a béchamel to the dark roux of a gumbo.

French cooking of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance prized costly spices, cinnamon, ginger, saffron and grains of paradise, often with sugar and verjuice, the sour juice of unripe grapes, in savoury dishes, and thickened its sauces with bread. La Varenne uses far less spice. He asks for butter, fresh herbs and vegetables such as asparagus, artichokes and mushrooms, cooked so that they taste of themselves. That turn towards the natural taste of the food is why historians call his book the first great book of modern French cooking.

Treat every claimed first with caution. It was not the first French cookbook: Le Viandier, credited to Taillevent, is some three centuries older. Nor did La Varenne invent stock, roux or herbs; he wrote down, clearly and in order, what good noble kitchens were doing. Duxelles shows the danger best. The name duxelles is not found in the book and is recorded only much later, so the story that he named it for his patron is tradition, not record. Say an early roux, never the first.

His name rarely comes up at the table, but his words do. When a guest asks what duxelles is, say finely chopped mushrooms and shallots cooked down in butter until dry, said to be named for a seventeenth-century French marquis. Keep the history light and the claims modest.

faults.fault: Wet, loose duxelles
faults.cause: Taken off the heat before the mushrooms' water had steamed away.
faults.fix: Keep cooking, stirring, until the pan sizzles rather than bubbles and the paste holds together.

faults.fault: Soggy pastry round a Wellington
faults.cause: A duxelles that still held water, or one used warm.
faults.fix: Cook it fully dry and cool it on a tray before it meets the pastry.

faults.fault: Duxelles that stews pale and watery instead of cooking down
faults.cause: Too low a heat or too small a pan, so the mushrooms' water pools instead of steaming off.
faults.fix: Use a wide pan over medium to medium-high heat and keep stirring until it sizzles; season at the end, since the mushrooms lose more than half their volume and the salt concentrates.

faults.fault: Bitter, scorched shallot
faults.cause: The heat too high before the mushrooms went in.
faults.fix: Soften the shallot gently, without colour, then add the mushrooms.

cards.front: Who was La Varenne, and what book did he publish?
cards.back: François Pierre de La Varenne, a seventeenth-century French cook to the Marquis d'Uxelles, who published Le Cuisinier françois in Paris in 1651.

cards.front: Who was La Varenne's patron, and which preparation is said to carry his name?
cards.back: Louis Chalon du Blé, Marquis d'Uxelles. Duxelles, the mushroom and shallot hash, is said to be named for him, by tradition rather than record.

cards.front: How did La Varenne's cooking break with medieval French cooking?
cards.back: Far fewer costly spices and less sugar in savoury food, and fewer bread-thickened sauces; instead butter, fresh herbs and vegetables cooked to taste of themselves.

cards.front: What does La Varenne build his dishes and sauces on?
cards.back: The bouillon, a broth of meat, bones and vegetables kept ready to cook and moisten other dishes, as stock underpins a sauce today.

cards.front: What does reducing a stock by half do?
cards.back: Water steams away and flavour concentrates: 1 litre (about 1 quart) becomes 500 ml (about 2 cups), deeper and fuller but still thin; season only after reducing.

cards.front: What thickener does Le Cuisinier françois keep ready for sauces?
cards.back: A liaison of flour browned in melted lard, among the earliest printed forms of what cooks soon called roux.

cards.front: What is a bouquet garni, and why is it tied?
cards.back: A bundle of herbs, usually parsley stalks, thyme and bay, tied so it flavours a pot and lifts out whole. La Varenne's herb bundles are its ancestor.

cards.front: How do you make duxelles?
cards.back: Chop mushrooms and shallot fine, soften the shallot in butter, then cook the mushrooms for 10 to 15 minutes until all their water has steamed away.

cards.front: Why must duxelles be cooked completely dry?
cards.back: Water left in it steams inside pastry or a stuffing and turns it soggy; a dry duxelles keeps a beef Wellington crust crisp.

cards.front: When did Le Cuisinier françois reach English readers?
cards.back: In 1653, two years after the French original, as The French Cook; the book was reprinted again and again.

cards.front: Why be careful calling La Varenne's book the first of anything?
cards.back: Le Viandier is some three centuries older, and he set down what good kitchens already did: say an early roux, not the first.

entries.title: Carême
entries.summary: Marie-Antoine Carême (1784 to 1833), the Paris pastry cook who rose to cook for Talleyrand, the Prince Regent, Tsar Alexander I and the Rothschilds. He built sugar architecture, sorted sauces into four great families and set grand cooking down in books.
entries.guest: Carême was the celebrated Paris chef of Napoleon's time, famous for towering sugar centrepieces and for sorting French sauces into the families cooks still learn.

paras: Marie-Antoine Carême, who called himself Antonin, is often called the first celebrity chef, a claim to hold as loosely as any first. Born into a poor Paris family in 1784, he was abandoned as a young boy in the Revolutionary years of the 1790s and found work in a cheap eating house. From 1798 he was apprenticed to Sylvain Bailly, a fashionable pastry cook in the rue Vivienne, and pastry made his name. He died in Paris in 1833, not yet fifty.
He matters to a cook today for two reasons: he showed that the grandest cooking could be organised and taught, and he left a system of sauces every later kitchen built on.

Bailly let him study architecture engravings at the national library nearby, and Carême turned temples, pavilions, ruins and fountains into sugar centrepieces for the shop window. They won him grand patrons. He cooked for years for Talleyrand, Napoleon's foreign minister, at his Paris house and at the Château de Valençay; then for the Prince Regent, the future George IV, in England; for Tsar Alexander I of Russia; and in his last working years for James de Rothschild in Paris. He was called the king of chefs and the chef of kings.

He wrote as hard as he cooked. Le Pâtissier royal parisien and Le Pâtissier pittoresque set out his pastry and his drawings, and Le Maître d'hôtel français and Le Cuisinier parisien followed. His last work, L'Art de la cuisine française au dix-neuvième siècle, began to appear in 1833, the year he died; its final two volumes were written after his death by his follower Armand Plumerey. Together the books codified haute cuisine, the grand cooking of great houses: they named dishes, fixed methods and drew the plates, so the style could be learned from a page.

A pièce montée, a mounted piece, is an architectural centrepiece of sugar and pastry built for a banquet table. It is drawn first and built in parts. Pastillage, a paste of icing sugar bound with gelatine or gum, is rolled thin, cut to templates and dried hard for a day or more. Spun sugar, nougat, marzipan and pastry add colour and texture, and the parts are joined with royal icing or with caramel cooked to a light amber, about 160 to 170°C (320 to 338°F), which sets hard as it cools. The croquembouche, a cone of choux puffs glued with caramel, is the pièce montée still made for French weddings and christenings.

Carême brought the same order to sauces. In his scheme four great sauces, espagnole, velouté, allemande and béchamel, head the families, and the smaller sauces descend from them by adding a flavour, a garnish or an enrichment. Espagnole is the brown base, velouté the pale one built on white stock, allemande a velouté bound with egg yolk, and béchamel, in his day a velouté reduced with cream rather than the milk and roux sauce cooks make now. The tree itself, and how Escoffier later changed it, belong to their own entries. The lesson here is the idea: a kitchen works from a few prepared bases rather than inventing every sauce from nothing.

Sugar work fails in a few known ways. Caramel cooked past a light amber turns dark and bitter and cannot be lightened, so start again. Syrup taken off before the hard crack, about 150°C (302°F), or a humid room, leaves the joins sticky: keep the work dry and assemble close to the event. Pastillage rolled unevenly or dried on one side cracks and warps, so roll it even and turn the pieces as they dry.

Treat the stories with care. Carême is often credited with the tall white chef's toque, but cooks wore caps long before him and the evidence for his part is thin. The tale that Talleyrand set him a year of menus with no dish repeated, using only the season's produce, rests on retelling. Tell both as legends. If a guest asks why French sauce names fill a New Orleans menu, the line runs from Carême's families through Escoffier to the house's sauces: the marchand de vin descends from the brown sauce, espagnole, while the hollandaise and béarnaise belong to the warm egg and butter sauces that later teaching made a fifth family.

entries.title: Escoffier
entries.summary: Georges Auguste Escoffier (1846 to 1935) ran the kitchens of César Ritz's hotels, organised the kitchen into stations and set the classical repertoire down in Le Guide culinaire of 1903, simplifying Carême's grand style for the restaurant.
entries.guest: Escoffier was the French chef who organised the modern restaurant kitchen. He is credited with peach Melba and Melba toast, and the sauce families on our plates follow his book.

paras: Auguste Escoffier is a large part of the reason a professional kitchen looks and sounds the way it does. Born in 1846 in Villeneuve-Loubet, a village near Nice, he went into his uncle's restaurant kitchen in Nice at thirteen and cooked until he retired in 1920. He did three things every cook still lives with: he organised the kitchen into stations working at the same time, he wrote the classical repertoire down in one book, and he made Carême's grand cooking lighter and quicker for the restaurant. He died in Monte Carlo in 1935.

In the 1880s he joined the Swiss hotelier César Ritz. From 1890 the two ran the Savoy in London, Ritz in the dining room and Escoffier in the kitchen; then came the Ritz in Paris, opened in 1898, and the Carlton in London, where Escoffier cooked for some two decades. Le Guide culinaire, first published in Paris in 1903 with his colleagues Philéas Gilbert and Émile Fétu, gathered the repertoire into numbered recipes, some five thousand in later editions. It kept Carême's bases and families but cleared away ornament: fewer garnishes, lighter sauces, dishes served hot, course by course. It reached English in 1907 as A Guide to Modern Cookery.

Escoffier divided the kitchen into parties, or stations, each led by a chef de partie: the saucier for sauces and sautés, the rôtisseur for roasts, the poissonnier for fish, the entremetier for vegetables and eggs, the garde manger for cold work and the pâtissier for pastry. The example often told is a plate of eggs with a grilled kidney and truffle sauce: one cook alone needed about a quarter of an hour, while three stations working at once let the chef assemble it in minutes. At the pass, the counter where finished plates leave the kitchen, the aboyeur, the caller, reads each ticket aloud so every station starts, or fires, its part together. The full brigade has its own entry.

His grandes sauces de base, the great base sauces, are four: espagnole, velouté, béchamel and tomate. Hollandaise is in the Guide, but among the smaller sauces that follow, not among the bases. The tidy list of five mother sauces, hollandaise beside the four, is later teaching; learn both and say which you mean.

Dishes credited to him: peach Melba, poached peaches on vanilla ice cream, later with raspberry purée, made at the Savoy for the soprano Nellie Melba; Melba toast, the thin slice toasted twice, also named for her; and Cherries Jubilee, cherries in thickened syrup lit with warm kirsch, made for one of Queen Victoria's jubilees, usually said to be 1897, with no ice cream at all. Sole Véronique, sole poached in white wine with peeled white grapes and glazed, is his by kitchen tradition, said to be named for André Messager's operetta Véronique; tellings differ on the year and the cook.

The house teaches its menus as a lesson in Escoffier's sauce families: hollandaise on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen; béarnaise on the breakfast hanger steak; Choron, a béarnaise with tomato, on the Eggs Sardou; Foyot, a béarnaise with meat glaze, on the Chateaubriand; and marchand de vin, the red wine sauce, from the brown side. Its advice is to learn the sauce on each plate first, because the sauce usually matters more than the protein.

The Redfish Véronique borrows his sole Véronique and makes three swaps: Louisiana redfish for sole, hibiscus-pickled grapes for fresh ones and a preserved lemon beurre blanc for the glazed sauce. Cherries Jubilee is printed as fresh tart black cherries in a Luxardo sauce, flamed at the table over housemade vanilla ice cream, but it was not on the dessert menu of 3 October 2026: confirm with a manager before offering it.

At the table, Escoffier is a one-line story: the chef who organised the restaurant kitchen and wrote its rules, whose sauce families explain our egg dishes. If a guest calls hollandaise a mother sauce, agree that most kitchens teach it so; there is no need to correct a guest, but know what the Guide itself says.

brennans.how: Credited to Escoffier for one of Queen Victoria's jubilees, usually said to be 1897. Ours is fresh tart black cherries in a Luxardo sauce, flamed at the table over housemade vanilla ice cream; it was off the 3 October 2026 dessert menu, so confirm with a manager first.

The Eggs Hussarde carries the lesson on one plate: hollandaise, the yolk and butter sauce, with marchand de vin, the red wine sauce from the brown side. Learn the sauce first and the description follows.

entries.title: The roots of Creole cooking
entries.say: As it reads: the roots of Creole cooking.
entries.summary: Creole cooking is the cooking of New Orleans: French at its base and built by many hands, Spanish rulers, West African and Caribbean cooks, Native American neighbours, German and Italian settlers. The Acadians gave rise to its country cousin, Cajun.
entries.guest: Creole cooking is New Orleans in a pot: French technique with Spanish, West African, Caribbean, Native American, German and Italian hands. Our gumbo tells the story in one bowl.

paras: Creole cooking is the city's own cooking, and Brennan's is a Creole house. It is French at its base, but no single people made it. Spanish governors, West African cooks brought in slavery, refugees from the Caribbean, Native American neighbours, and later German and Italian settlers all added ingredients and skills. Knowing who brought what lets you explain a dish in one honest sentence, and reminds you whose hands built this food.

French. New Orleans was founded for France in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville. France gave the kitchen its grammar: technique, sauces built on stock, a habit of good bread and pastry, and the roux, flour cooked slowly in fat to thicken a pot. The roux is the clearest inheritance, though Louisiana cooks took it far darker than any Paris kitchen.

Spanish. Louisiana passed to Spain in the 1760s and stayed Spanish until 1803, when it went briefly back to France and then to the United States. Spanish cooks favoured peppers, tomatoes and rice cooked in one pan with meat and seasoning, and jambalaya is often called a cousin of paella.

West African. From 1719 French ships carried enslaved Africans to Louisiana, many from the rice-growing country of Senegal and the Gambia. With them came okra, whose African name most likely gave gumbo its own, along with the skill of growing and cooking rice, deep frying and the one-pot stew served over a starch. Enslaved and later free Black cooks did most of the cooking in the city's kitchens for generations: Creole food is their creation as much as anyone's.

Caribbean. In 1809 and 1810 more than ten thousand refugees from Saint-Domingue, the French colony that became Haiti, reached New Orleans by way of Cuba, which had expelled them, and doubled the city's population within months. White, free people of colour and enslaved in nearly equal numbers, they brought cooks from French Caribbean kitchens, where French, African and island cooking had already met.

Native American. The Choctaw and their neighbours gave the colony filé, ground dried sassafras leaves, often said to have been sold for generations at the French Market, and the corn, beans and squash the first settlers lived on. Many accounts add the bay leaf, since the Gulf South has native bay trees.

German and Italian. From the 1720s German farmers settled the German Coast upriver and fed the city; their sausage making is often credited with shaping Louisiana andouille, a smoked pork sausage French by name, and their mustard with Creole mustard. From the 1880s Sicilian immigrants filled the French Quarter's markets and groceries, and the muffuletta, a round Sicilian loaf filled with cured meats, cheese and olive salad, is usually credited to Central Grocery on Decatur Street.

The Acadians. From 1755 the British expelled French settlers from Acadia, in today's Maritime provinces of Canada, chiefly Nova Scotia; from the 1760s many reached Louisiana and settled west of the city. Their country cooking is the root of Cajun food, a cousin with its own entry.

At Brennan's, the Seafood Gumbo is the roots in one bowl, and the house teaches it that way: a name taken from an African word for okra, ki ngombo in the Bantu languages of west-central Africa, a French roux taken darker in Louisiana, filé from the Choctaw, and Spanish, German and Caribbean cooks adding their part. Ours is shrimp, crab, oysters and andouille over popcorn rice. Whether tonight's pot carries okra or filé is a lineup question.

Keep it short at the table: French technique, many hands. Name two or three strands and point to the plate, the roux, the rice, the peppers. Never tell it as a French story alone; the cooks of African descent who did the work belong in the first sentence, not the last.

entries.title: Lafcadio Hearn's La Cuisine Créole
entries.summary: La Cuisine Créole, printed in 1885 and generally credited to Lafcadio Hearn, is among the first books of Creole cooking: a record of gumbos, courtbouillon, jambalaya and sauces as New Orleans cooked them while a world's fair filled the city.
entries.guest: La Cuisine Créole is one of the first Creole cookbooks, printed in 1885 and generally credited to the writer Lafcadio Hearn. Gumbo is already in its pages, as it is on our menu today.

paras: La Cuisine Créole is a New Orleans cookbook printed in 1885 and generally credited to the writer Lafcadio Hearn. Its subtitle promised recipes from leading chefs and noted Creole housewives, and it reads as a snapshot of the city's kitchens at the time: gumbos, courtbouillon (said coo-bee-YON in New Orleans: fish simmered in a roux and tomato gravy, not the French court-bouillon, the quick aromatic liquid fish is poached in), jambalaya, soups, sauces, breads, sweets and drinks.

It matters because it is among the first printed witnesses that Creole cooking was already a cuisine of its own, French in method and New Orleans in its larder, decades before Galatoire's, Arnaud's or Brennan's opened. When a guest asks how old a dish or a word is, books like this are where a good answer starts.

Hearn was born in 1850 on the Greek island of Lefkada, to a Greek mother and an Irish father, and grew up largely in Dublin. He came to the United States as a young man, worked as a newspaper reporter in Cincinnati and moved to New Orleans in 1877. For about ten years he wrote for the city's papers and collected its stories, songs and Creole sayings, then left for the French West Indies and, in 1890, for Japan, where he took the name Koizumi Yakumo.

The book came out in 1885, while the World's Industrial and Cotton Centennial Exposition, the world's fair that opened in New Orleans in December 1884, was drawing visitors to the city. It carried no author's name: Hearn's authorship is generally accepted rather than printed on the title page, so say generally credited to Hearn. The same year the Christian Woman's Exchange, a New Orleans women's charity, published its own Creole Cookery Book.

Two Creole cookbooks in one year is why careful historians call them among the first books of Creole cooking rather than the first. Which reached readers earlier is not settled, and in food history a claimed first rarely survives a closer look.

The recipes are short paragraphs written for a cook who already knew the work. Measures are loose by modern standards, spoonfuls and pints rather than grams, and an oven is hot, moderate or slow rather than set to a number. Behind the words sit wood and coal stoves, lard and butter, and seafood brought in daily from the lake and the Gulf.

To cook from it, work as a chef works with any old recipe. Read it twice and name the method: a roux and a stew, a boil, a bake. Translate the measures: a US pint is about 475 ml and a tablespoon about 15 ml. Read a hot oven as roughly 205 to 220°C (400 to 425°F) and a moderate one as roughly 175 to 190°C (350 to 375°F). Cook a half batch, taste, and write the result down in grams, degrees, minutes and yield. Then take it to the chef: the book is evidence, and the chef's recipe is the standard.

Three mistakes come up on the floor. Calling it the first Creole cookbook forgets the Exchange's book of the same year. Saying Hearn signed it forgets that no author's name is printed on it. Treating its recipes as exact forgets more than a century of change in stoves, ingredients and food safety: test them, never copy them.

Brennan's opened in 1946, sixty-one years after the book, but the line runs straight. Gumbo is already in Hearn's pages, and our Seafood Gumbo, with shrimp, crab, oysters and andouille over popcorn rice, belongs to the tradition he recorded. Never tell a guest that a dish of ours is a recipe from the book: the book shows where a dish comes from, and the kitchen says how ours is made today.

At the table, a sentence or two is plenty: one of the first Creole cookbooks, from 1885, generally credited to Lafcadio Hearn, the writer later famous in Japan. Book lovers often know his Japanese writing and enjoy hearing about his New Orleans years. Never present a recipe from it as ours, and send any question about how a Brennan's dish is made today to the kitchen.

entries.title: The Picayune's Creole Cook Book
entries.summary: The Picayune's Creole Cook Book, published by the Daily Picayune around 1900, set down the cooking of the city's Black Creole cooks. Reprinted for decades, it is a source for dishes and words, not a set of exact modern recipes.
entries.guest: The Picayune newspaper published a Creole cookbook around 1900 to record the cooking of the city's Black Creole cooks. It was reprinted for decades, with gumbos, grillades and pralines in it.

paras: The Picayune's Creole Cook Book is a large collection of New Orleans recipes published by the city's newspaper, the Daily Picayune. Sources date the first edition to 1900 or 1901, and the early printings are scarce, so say around 1900 unless you have checked a copy; the text most often reprinted today is a 1901 edition.

It matters because it is one of the fullest early records of Creole home cooking, and because of whose cooking it records: the book set out to write down the methods of the Black Creole cooks of old New Orleans, with those of the old Creole housekeepers, before they were lost. Many dishes on the city's menus today can be traced through its pages.

Its preface explains the purpose. With the end of slavery, it says, the old Creole cooks and their knowledge were passing out of the households that had depended on them, and the paper wanted their methods on record. Teach this plainly. The skill in the book was largely the skill of Black cooks, while the preface looks back on the households of slavery with nostalgia and speaks of Black cooks in language that reads as offensive today. Read it with care and context, and never repeat that language at the table.

The book kept selling. Editions followed through the 1900s, 1910s, 1920s and 1930s, and on through the middle of the century and beyond, so the editions read side by side show how Creole cooking changed over the twentieth century.

Gumbos come in many forms, thickened with filé or okra, alongside a gumbo made with greens. Courtbouillon, said coo-bee-YON, is fish, often redfish, simmered in a roux and tomato gravy; it shares a name, but not a method, with the French court-bouillon, the light aromatic liquid fish is poached in. Grillades are thin slices of veal or beef browned and simmered in a rich gravy, eaten with grits. Pralines are the pecan and sugar sweets the city still sells, and café brûlot is coffee flamed with brandy, spice and citrus peel. Jambalaya, soups, breads and a long run of cakes and sweets are there too.

Use it as a source for dishes and words, not as a set of exact modern recipes. Its cooks judged by eye, smell and long practice, and its measures, stoves and ingredients belong to another century. Its spellings of French and Creole dish names are worth learning, since the city still uses many of them.

When a recipe catches the chef's eye, read it through and name the method. Translate the measures into grams and millilitres. Put a temperature on every judgement the book makes by eye: pralines, for example, go to the soft-ball stage, 112 to 116°C (234 to 241°F) on a sugar thermometer, where an old cook tested a drop of syrup in cold water. Bring modern food safety to it, cooling and holding included. Then cook a half batch, taste, and write it down with a yield for the chef.
The usual slips: giving one firm date for the first edition, cooking a recipe word for word, quoting the preface aloud, or saying the Picayune invented dishes it only recorded.

Brennan's does not pour café brûlot, but its Café Brûlot Coffee Cake borrows the drink's flavours: chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate cake, pecans, a spiced citrus glaze and whipped crème fraîche. Sell it as the coffee's flavours, not the flame. When pralines come up, say them the house way: PRAH-leen, never PRAY-leen.

At the table: a cookbook the Picayune newspaper published around 1900 to record the cooking of the city's Black Creole cooks, reprinted for decades. If a guest asks whether a Brennan's dish comes from it, do not guess. The honest answer is that the old cookbooks show where these dishes come from, and the kitchen can say how ours is made today.

entries.title: Antoine's
entries.summary: Antoine's, founded in 1840 by Antoine Alciatore of Marseille, calls itself the oldest family-run restaurant in the United States. It is credited with Oysters Rockefeller, café brûlot and Eggs Sardou, and a novel about it inspired Breakfast at Brennan's.
entries.guest: Antoine's opened in 1840 and calls itself the oldest family-run restaurant in the country. Our Eggs Sardou began there; we make it the Brennan's way, with Choron sauce.

paras: Antoine's is a French Creole restaurant at 713 St. Louis Street in the French Quarter, founded in 1840 by Antoine Alciatore, a young cook from Marseille. It calls itself the oldest family-run restaurant in the United States, and the founder's descendants still run it.

For a cook and server at Brennan's it matters twice over. Dishes the whole city serves were born or named there, the Eggs Sardou on our breakfast menu among them, and a novel about the house gave Owen Brennan the idea that became Breakfast at Brennan's.

Alciatore came to New Orleans young and opened his restaurant in 1840, cooking French food with Louisiana ingredients. His son Jules, who took over the kitchen, made the house famous, and the family has run it through every generation since.

In 1948 Frances Parkinson Keyes published Dinner at Antoine's, a popular mystery novel set in New Orleans, and the title carried the house's name across the country. Owen Brennan took his cue from it and asked why not Breakfast at Brennan's; that story has its own entry.

Jules Alciatore is credited with three dishes the city still serves. Oysters Rockefeller, by the house's account created in 1889, are oysters baked on the half shell under a rich green sauce, named for John D. Rockefeller because the sauce was so rich; the recipe is still a house secret. Pompano en papillote is Gulf pompano baked in a sealed paper parcel. Café brûlot diabolique is brandy and orange liqueur flamed in a bowl with spice and citrus peel, then ladled into strong coffee. Each has its own entry.

Eggs Sardou was created there too, named in honour of the French playwright Victorien Sardou; sources disagree on the year. Antoine's original set poached eggs on artichoke bottoms, the cup-shaped base of the heart, with hollandaise, finished with ham, anchovy and truffle, and no spinach. Most later versions dropped the ham, anchovy and truffle for creamed spinach.

Antoine's is a warren of more than a dozen dining rooms, from grand rooms for banquets to small private ones, several of them named for Carnival krewes, the clubs that stage the parades and balls, such as Rex, and hung with the krewes' photographs and souvenirs. The menu is long and written in French, and waiters who stay for decades guide guests through it. Regulars keep their own waiter and ask for that waiter by name, a habit the old New Orleans houses share.

Three slips to avoid: crediting Antoine with the famous dishes, when the house credits his son Jules; calling Eggs Sardou a Brennan's invention; and telling a guest that Brennan's pours café brûlot, when our menu carries its flavours in a coffee cake.

The Eggs Sardou on our menu is Antoine's dish in the Brennan's style: crispy artichokes, Parmesan creamed spinach, poached eggs and Choron sauce, a béarnaise tinted with tomato, in place of hollandaise. Never present it as a Brennan's invention.

Guests often name Antoine's in the same breath as Brennan's. Speak of it warmly: it is the elder of the old French Quarter houses, a short walk from Royal Street, and the city's restaurants share a history rather than compete over it. When a guest orders the Sardou, one sentence is enough: created at Antoine's and named for the playwright Victorien Sardou, and made here the Brennan's way. Say the name AN-twahnz.

entries.title: Galatoire's
entries.summary: Galatoire's, opened on Bourbon Street in 1905 by Jean Galatoire, is the French Quarter house known for its customs: a line on the pavement for the downstairs room, the long Friday lunch, jackets in the evening and waiters kept for decades.
entries.guest: Galatoire's opened on Bourbon Street in 1905. The downstairs room is still first come, first served, the Friday lunch runs long, and their own site gives the dress code.

paras: Galatoire's is a French Creole restaurant at 209 Bourbon Street, opened in 1905 by Jean Galatoire and run by his family for generations. It is famous less for any one dish than for its customs: for most of its history it took no reservations for the downstairs room, so guests queued on the pavement, and its long Friday lunch is a New Orleans institution.
For a cook and server at Brennan's it is a lesson in what regulars value in an old house: the same room, the same waiter and the same plates, year after year.

Jean Galatoire, an immigrant from France, bought Victor's Restaurant on Bourbon Street in 1905 and gave it his name. His family has run it ever since, and with it the customs its regulars expect: the line, the long lunch and the waiter who knows the table. Brennan's has a Bourbon Street beginning of its own: Owen Brennan opened there in 1946, and the restaurant moved to 417 Royal Street in 1956.

For most of its life Galatoire's took no bookings at all. Everyone, regular or visitor, waited in line on the Bourbon Street pavement, and the line before Friday lunch became part of the city's social calendar, with some regulars paying a stand-in to hold their place. The upstairs dining rooms now take reservations, but the downstairs room is still first come, first served, and it is where the regulars want to be.

The Friday lunch is long, loud and sociable, with tables visiting tables, and it can run on into the evening. Regulars keep the same waiter for decades and often order on that waiter's advice rather than from the menu alone. As published, the house asks gentlemen for a jacket from 5 in the evening and all day on Sunday, and business casual at lunch; confirm the current rule on its own site before you advise a guest.

Four plates carry the house's name. Trout meunière amandine is a trout fillet dusted in seasoned flour and fried golden in clarified butter or oil, since whole butter burns before the fish is done, then finished with browned butter, lemon and toasted sliced almonds. Shrimp rémoulade is cold boiled shrimp in the New Orleans rémoulade, a spicy, mustardy sauce reddened with paprika. Crabmeat maison is lump crabmeat dressed with a mayonnaise sauce, capers and green onion. Soufflé potatoes are thin slices fried twice, at two heats, until they puff into hollow pillows, served with béarnaise for dipping. The trout and the potatoes each have their own entry.

The common slips: saying Galatoire's takes no reservations at all, when the upstairs rooms do; dating it with Antoine's, when it opened sixty-five years later; and advising a guest on dress from memory.

If a guest is going on to Galatoire's, help them plan: the downstairs line, the jacket rule in the evening, and a word that the Friday lunch runs long. If they ask about our own rule, the house standard is dressy casual, with jackets preferred at dinner. Speak of Galatoire's with respect; the old houses share their regulars, and a guest who loves one often loves the others.

entries.title: Arnaud's
entries.summary: Arnaud's, opened in 1918 by Arnaud Cazenave, a French wine salesman known as Count Arnaud, is one of the grand old French Creole houses of the French Quarter: Shrimp Arnaud, soufflé potatoes, flaming café brûlot and the French 75 Bar.
entries.guest: Arnaud's opened in 1918, a short walk from us on Bienville Street. It is known for Shrimp Arnaud, soufflé potatoes and its French 75 Bar, and it is worth an evening.

paras: Arnaud's is a French Creole restaurant at 813 Bienville Street in the French Quarter, a short walk from Royal Street. Arnaud Cazenave, a French wine salesman known to the city as Count Arnaud, opened it in 1918. Over the years he bought the buildings beside it and joined them, until the restaurant filled most of a city block.

It matters to a cook and server at Brennan's because its signatures, Shrimp Arnaud, Oysters Bienville, soufflé potatoes, café brûlot and crêpes Suzette, are the old Creole repertoire guests compare us with, and because, with Antoine's and Galatoire's, it is one of the grand houses guests name in the same breath as ours.

Count Arnaud ran the house for thirty years and died in 1948. His daughter, Germaine Cazenave Wells, took it over and ran it for the next three decades. She was a famous figure of Carnival, the season of balls and parades before Lent, and reigned as queen of more than twenty Mardi Gras balls. Her gowns and keepsakes fill the Germaine Cazenave Wells Mardi Gras Museum, opened upstairs at the restaurant in 1983.
In 1978 the house passed to Archie Casbarian, who restored the old buildings and their dining rooms. He died in 2009, and his family runs Arnaud's still.

Shrimp Arnaud is the house's shrimp rémoulade: boiled Gulf shrimp, chilled and dressed in a red Creole rémoulade, sharp with Creole mustard, paprika and horseradish, quite unlike the pale, mayonnaise-based French rémoulade. Oysters Bienville are oysters baked on the half shell under a thick, creamy sauce of chopped shrimp, mushrooms and green onion, crusted with breadcrumbs and cheese, named for Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville, who founded New Orleans in 1718. Arnaud's says it created the dish: tell that as the house's claim. Both dishes have their own entries.

Soufflé potatoes are thin slices of potato fried twice, first at a lower heat and then at a higher one, so they puff into hollow golden pillows; Arnaud's serves them with béarnaise for dipping. Café brûlot, brandy flamed with spice and citrus peel and ladled into strong coffee, and crêpes Suzette, thin pancakes warmed in an orange butter sauce and flamed with orange liqueur, are both made at the table.

Arnaud's runs as several rooms under one roof. The main dining room serves the classic menu; Arnaud's Jazz Bistro pairs dinner with live jazz; rooms upstairs take private parties and hold the museum. The café brûlot is the house's best-known piece of theatre: the waiter ladles the flaming brandy down a long spiral of orange peel studded with cloves into the bowl, and only then does the coffee go in.

The French 75 Bar takes its name from the cocktail, itself named for a French field gun of the First World War: a spirit shaken with lemon juice and sugar, then topped with Champagne. Arnaud's makes it with Cognac, where many bars use gin. Both are French 75s; know which one a guest means.

Three slips to avoid: telling Oysters Bienville's origin as settled history, when it is the house's own claim; saying Arnaud's invented soufflé potatoes, which all the old houses serve and whose legend is French; and making Count Arnaud a nobleman, when Count was the city's name for him.

Arnaud's and Brennan's share a repertoire. Both serve Creole turtle soup, a dark soup thickened with a brown roux; ours is printed as 100% turtle meat. Both flame at the table: Arnaud's flames its café brûlot and crêpes Suzette, and we flame our Bananas Foster on a guéridon, the tableside cart. Café brûlot itself is not on our list: our Café Brûlot Coffee Cake borrows its flavours, chicory coffee and chocolate with a spiced citrus glaze, so sell the flavours, not the flame.

Guests often come to us from Arnaud's, or are going there tonight: speak of it warmly, and never rank the houses. Say what each does well and what we are known for: breakfast, turtle soup and Bananas Foster at the table. A guest who loved the French 75 there might like the Flamingo, poured only in our Roost Bar: vodka and gin with dragonfruit, lemon and Taittinger Champagne; confirm it on shift. Say the name ar-NOHZ.

entries.title: Commander's Palace
entries.summary: Commander's Palace is the Garden District restaurant Emile Commander opened in the late nineteenth century, owned by members of the Brennan family since around 1970. Its kitchen was led by Paul Prudhomme and Emeril Lagasse, and it is a separate business from Brennan's.
entries.guest: Commander's Palace is the turquoise and white Garden District house run by another branch of the Brennan family. It is a separate restaurant from ours, famous for turtle soup and jazz brunch.

paras: Commander's Palace is a Creole restaurant in a turquoise and white Victorian house at 1403 Washington Avenue, on the corner of Coliseum Street in the Garden District, across from Lafayette Cemetery No. 1. Members of the Brennan family have owned it since around 1970, and it belongs to the side of the family that followed Ella Brennan.

For a server at Brennan's it matters because guests confuse the two houses all the time. They share a family name, a Creole repertoire and some history, but they are separate businesses, with their own owners, kitchens and menus. Saying so kindly is part of the job.

Emile Commander opened the restaurant on its corner in the late nineteenth century. Its founding is given as 1880 in many accounts and as 1893 in others. A food historian's reading of the records, a building put up in 1892 and a liquor licence sought in January 1893, favours the later date, so name both years or say the 1890s. Emile died in 1906, and the house passed through other hands before the Brennans came.

They arrived around 1970. Some accounts date the family's purchase to 1969; others give 1974, the year the family's split was settled, when Ella's side took Commander's Palace as its home and Owen Brennan's widow and sons kept Royal Street. Ella, with her brothers and sisters Dick, Adelaide, John and Dottie, made it a national name.

Its kitchen became a school for famous chefs. Paul Prudhomme ran it from 1975, before opening K-Paul's Louisiana Kitchen in 1979; Emeril Lagasse followed him in the 1980s; Jamie Shannon led it through the 1990s until his death in 2001; Tory McPhail took over in the early 2000s; and Meg Bickford, who followed him, became the first woman to lead that kitchen. Prudhomme has his own entry.
Turtle soup is a house calling card: a dark, roux-thickened Creole soup with a splash of sherry added at the table.

The bread pudding soufflé is New Orleans bread pudding folded into a soufflé, served with a warm whiskey sauce poured into its centre at the table; it has its own entry. The weekend jazz brunch, with a small band moving from table to table, made the house a place to celebrate as much as to eat.

Here is the family in three sentences. Owen Brennan opened the first Brennan's on Bourbon Street in 1946, with his younger sister Ella learning the business beside him. After a split in the 1970s, settled in 1974, Owen's widow and sons kept Brennan's on Royal Street and Ella's side took Commander's Palace; Brennan's of Houston belongs to Ella's side too. Our house closed in 2013 and reopened in November 2014 under Ralph Brennan, a cousin, and his partner Terry White, and it is part of the Ralph Brennan Restaurant Group.

Both houses serve Creole turtle soup. Ours is printed as 100% turtle meat, made with farm-raised Louisiana freshwater turtle and served with brown butter spinach, grated egg and a splash of aged sherry. How it compares with theirs is a question for the kitchen, never a comparison made at the table.

Three mix-ups to avoid. Do not tell a guest that Brennan's owns Commander's Palace, or the other way round: they are separate businesses. Do not take sides in the family's split or the 2013 closure; say the family divided its restaurants in the 1970s, and a cousin bought this house and brought it back. And do not give one founding year as certain: 1880 and 1893 are both in print.

When a guest says they loved the bread pudding soufflé at Brennan's last night, they mean Commander's. Smile, and put it simply: that is a cousin's house in the Garden District, Commander's Palace, with the same family name and a separate kitchen; here on Royal Street we are known for breakfast, turtle soup and Bananas Foster at the table. Then offer our own New Orleans Bread Pudding, with whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream and pralines. Recommend Commander's warmly when asked.

entries.title: Owen and Ella Brennan
entries.say: As it reads: Owen and Ella Brennan.
entries.summary: Owen Brennan opened the restaurant on Bourbon Street in 1946; his younger sister Ella carried it to 417 Royal Street after his death and later led Commander's Palace. Their story, told briefly and accurately, sits behind every signature plate.
entries.guest: Owen Brennan opened on Bourbon Street in 1946. After he died, his sister Ella and the family moved the restaurant here, to 417 Royal Street, in 1956.

paras: Owen and Ella Brennan are the brother and sister at the start of our story. Owen founded the restaurant in 1946. Ella, his younger sister, learned the business beside him, carried it through his early death and became one of the great figures of American hospitality.

Every server needs this story in two sizes: a long one for a curious table, and a short one, four sentences, for a busy brunch. It explains our name, our address, our breakfast and our flaming dessert.

Owen Brennan was an Irish-American New Orleanian who already ran the Old Absinthe House, a bar on Bourbon Street. In July 1946 he opened his own restaurant across the street, Owen Brennan's Vieux Carré; Vieux Carré, old square, is the French Quarter's French name. The house legend says a rival teased him that an Irishman's cooking stopped at boiled potatoes, and Owen set out to prove otherwise with French and Creole cooking.

Owen noticed that most New Orleans restaurants served only lunch and dinner. Taking his cue from the popular novel Dinner at Antoine's, he asked why not Breakfast at Brennan's, and built a long, celebratory morning meal: an eye opener, which is a morning drink, then a soup, an egg dish and a flamed dessert. In 1951, at Owen's request, his chef Paul Blangé created Bananas Foster, with Ella beside him in the house's own telling, and it was named for Owen's friend Richard Foster.

A lease dispute in 1954 pushed Owen to plan a move to Royal Street. He died in November 1955, before the new house opened. Ella and the family finished the move, and the restaurant opened at 417 Royal Street in 1956.

Ella Brennan, born in 1925, began working for Owen as a young woman. After his death she held the family's restaurant together. When the family split in November 1973, settled in 1974, Owen's widow Maude and their sons Pip, Jimmy and Ted kept Royal Street, and Ella's side took Commander's Palace in the Garden District, which has its own entry. There, as Miss Ella to the city, she and her brothers and sisters made the house a national name and gave young chefs their start, Paul Prudhomme and Emeril Lagasse among them. She died in 2018.

Brennan's closed in June 2013 after a foreclosure and a family dispute. Ralph Brennan, a cousin of the former owners, and his partner Terry White bought the building at auction, later acquired the name, and restored the house from top to bottom, reopening in November 2014.

The pink house at 417 Royal Street was built in 1795, after the great fire. It later became the Banque de la Louisiane, the first bank in Louisiana, and the bank's initials, LB, still sit in the ironwork at the centre of the balcony railing. From 1841 to 1891 the Morphy family owned it, and Paul Morphy, the chess prodigy, lived there.

During the 2014 restoration the builders found turtles living in the courtyard, and the house adopted them. Ten live there now, named for sauces: five for the French mother sauces as kitchens teach them, Béchamel, Velouté, Espagnole, Tomate and Hollandaise, and five for New Orleans sauces. Each spring they parade to the fountain in what the house calls the slowest second line on earth; a second line is the New Orleans street parade that dances behind a brass band.

The short version, for a busy table: Owen Brennan opened on Bourbon Street in 1946. Bananas Foster was created there, at his request, in 1951. He died in 1955, and his sister Ella and the family moved the restaurant here in 1956. Ralph Brennan, a cousin, restored and reopened the house in 2014. And 2026 is our eightieth year, marked with two $80 tasting menus: quote them only from the printed card in your hand at lineup.

Three cautions. Tell the boiled potatoes story as the house legend it is. Do not tell a guest that Eggs Owen was named for Owen until a manager confirms it at lineup. And when a guest asks about the family split or the 2013 closure, keep it short and kind: the family divided its restaurants in the 1970s, and a cousin bought this house and brought it back. If a guest ordering turtle soup glances at the courtyard, say it with a smile: the soup is not the turtles.

entries.title: Paul Blangé
entries.summary: Paul Blangé, the Dutch-born first chef of Brennan's, led its kitchen from 1946 into the 1970s and created Bananas Foster in 1951, at Owen Brennan's request. His story teaches how to credit a dish: created here, credited with, or made famous here.
entries.guest: Paul Blangé was our first chef. In 1951 he created Bananas Foster at Owen Brennan's request, for a dinner honouring Owen's friend Richard Foster.

paras: Paul Blangé was the first chef of Brennan's, a Dutch-born cook who ran the kitchen from the restaurant's opening on Bourbon Street in 1946 into the 1970s. In 1951, at Owen Brennan's request, he created Bananas Foster, the dessert the server guide calls the most-ordered on the menu; confirm that claim at lineup before repeating it. The house credits him with more of its classics.
For a Sous Chef his story is a lesson in two things: what a head chef gives a house, a repertoire and the cooks who carry it on, and how carefully a kitchen must speak about who created what.

Blangé was born in the Netherlands in 1900 and came to New Orleans in 1922, where he cooked in several of the city's restaurants. In 1946 he became the first chef of Owen Brennan's Vieux Carré. He stayed through the move to 417 Royal Street in 1956 and led the kitchen into the 1970s. He died in 1977.

A chef's longest work is the cooks he trains. Michael Roussel started in the Brennan's kitchen in 1956, trained under Blangé, became executive chef in 1974 and retired in 2005 after 49 years. Lazone Randolph, who began as a dishwasher in 1965, followed him in 2005 and gave his name to Chicken Lazone. Since the 2014 reopening, Slade Rushing, Ryan Hacker and, from June 2025, Kris Padalino have led the kitchen. So the repertoire Blangé set down has passed from hand to hand for eighty years.

Bananas Foster shows how a house dish is born. In 1951 Owen Brennan asked for a new dessert for a dinner honouring his friend Richard Foster, chairman of the New Orleans Crime Commission. In the house's own telling, Ella and Blangé adapted the caramelised bananas the Brennans' mother made at home and named the dish for Foster. Bananas made sense: New Orleans was the main port of entry for bananas from Central and South America.

The tellings differ in one detail. The server guide has Owen challenging Blangé; the house's own pages, and Ralph Brennan, credit Ella with Blangé. Ask at lineup which telling the house prefers, and which name it uses for the commission, which is also called the Metropolitan Crime Commission.

Today the dish is built at the table from a short list of parts: butter, brown sugar and cinnamon melted into a caramel, the bananas, then rum, flamed and spooned over housemade vanilla ice cream. The menu prints rum; the house's published recipe adds banana liqueur too, so confirm the cart build at lineup. The method has its own entry.

Credit is where servers slip. Bananas Foster was created here, in 1951: say so with confidence. Eggs Hussarde is different. The house credits Blangé with it, and with Chicken Pontalba, but a recipe for poached eggs à la Hussarde was printed in 1895, credited to the chef Adolphe Gallier of the Hotel Brunswick in New York, and Escoffier gave a version in 1903. Brennan's made the dish famous from about 1950: it is our signature, never our invention, and the house's wording is confirmed at lineup.
Stories also grow around a famous cook. You may hear that Blangé was buried with a Brennan's menu. No source we trust confirms it, so do not tell it to a guest as fact.

Blangé's name lives at the table through two plates. Bananas Foster is flamed at the table on a guéridon, the tableside cart, with a minimum of two per order, and 2026 is its 75th year. Eggs Hussarde, the house's signature egg dish, sets poached eggs on Canadian bacon over a toasted base, with marchand de vin, the red wine sauce, beneath and hollandaise on top.

Say his name blahn-ZHAY. When a guest asks who created Bananas Foster, one sentence carries it: our first chef, Paul Blangé, in 1951, at Owen Brennan's request, named for Owen's friend Richard Foster. Use the telling the house confirms at lineup. When a guest asks whether Eggs Hussarde was invented here, say it is our signature and New Orleans' answer to Eggs Benedict, made famous here, from a recipe older than the restaurant.

entries.title: Paul Prudhomme
entries.summary: Paul Prudhomme (1940 to 2015), a Cajun farm boy from near Opelousas, ran the kitchen at Commander's Palace from 1975, opened K-Paul's in 1979, created blackened redfish and taught the country to cook Louisiana food.
entries.guest: Paul Prudhomme was the Cajun chef who made blackening famous at K-Paul's in the French Quarter around 1980. Our Blackened Tofu uses his method on local tofu.

paras: Paul Prudhomme is the reason a diner in Ohio or California knows the words Cajun and blackened. He was born in 1940 on his family's farm near Opelousas, on the Cajun prairie of St. Landry Parish, the youngest of thirteen children, and learnt to cook in his mother's kitchen. For a generation of Americans he was the face of Louisiana cooking: chef, restaurateur, creator of blackened redfish, maker of seasoning blends and teacher through his books and television. He died in New Orleans in 2015, at seventy-five.

In 1975 he became executive chef, the head of the kitchen, at Commander's Palace in the Garden District, run by Ella Brennan's side of the family. In 1979 he and his wife, Kay, known as K, opened K-Paul's Louisiana Kitchen on Chartres Street in the French Quarter, where he cooked and she ran the dining room; the K in the name is hers. Around 1980 he created blackened redfish there: a fillet dipped in butter, coated in spice and seared in a dry cast-iron pan so hot the spices toast almost black. The method has its own entry.

The dish became a national craze. Restaurants everywhere put blackened fish, and soon anything called Cajun, on their menus, and so many cooks wanted redfish that the Gulf stock fell; Louisiana closed its commercial redfish fishery in the late 1980s. K-Paul's closed for good in 2020.

His cooking rests on seasoning built in layers. He taught that black, white and red pepper each strike a different part of the mouth, so he used them together, with salt, garlic, onion, paprika and dried herbs, added in stages. A cook working in his style seasons the vegetables as they soften, again when the liquid goes in, and tastes before the last adjustment, so the heat builds through the dish instead of sitting on top.

He also made his roux fast. Heat oil in a heavy cast-iron pan until it just smokes, whisk in flour, roughly equal weights of each, and keep whisking: the roux turns a deep red-brown in three to five minutes, and the chopped vegetables go in at once to cool it and stop the browning. Hot roux sticks to skin and burns, so learn the slow roux first and try his only beside a chef.

Magic Seasoning Blends began with guests at K-Paul's asking to buy the blends the kitchen mixed for itself; in 1983 he founded a company to sell them. His cookbooks, starting with Chef Paul Prudhomme's Louisiana Kitchen in 1984, gave home cooks clear instructions for gumbo, étouffée and jambalaya. His restaurant and his first book both carry the words Louisiana Kitchen, and that was his point: the Cajun cooking of his childhood had met the Creole city, and to the rest of the country the two became one Louisiana cooking.

He also carried a phrase. The holy trinity, onion, celery and green pepper, is believed to have been popularised by him in the early 1980s; some accounts say he coined it, but none proves it, so say popularised. The trinity has its own entry.

Fame brought imitation, and the imitations' faults teach his method. Cayenne alone gives heat with no flavour: use a layered blend. Seasoning thrown in at the end sits harsh on the tongue: season in stages and taste. And Cajun does not mean burnt or fiery: it is the Acadians' country cooking of smoked meat, dark roux and rice, seasoned with care.

At Brennan's his technique reaches the menu through the Blackened Tofu: local Tien Dat tofu, blackened, over Two Brooks Farm rice grits with preserved shiitake mushrooms. The house tells it simply: his small kitchen had no grill, so the hot pan imitated char. The classic method uses butter, so never call the dish vegan until the kitchen confirms it at lineup.

For a guest, Prudhomme is one line: the Cajun chef who made blackening famous at K-Paul's and sent Louisiana food around the country. If a guest says blackened means burnt, explain that the spices are toasted dark in a very hot pan while the inside stays moist. Questions about the heat, the butter or the spice blend go to the kitchen.

entries.title: Leah Chase
entries.summary: Leah Chase (1923 to 2019), the Queen of Creole Cuisine, cooked for some seven decades at Dooky Chase's in Tremé, feeding civil rights leaders, presidents and her neighbours, and showed that Creole cooking is a Black Creole tradition.
entries.guest: Leah Chase was the Queen of Creole Cuisine, chef at Dooky Chase's in Tremé for some seven decades, remembered for her fried chicken and her Holy Thursday gumbo z'herbes.

paras: Leah Chase is the cook to name whenever someone asks whose cooking Creole cooking is. Born in New Orleans in 1923 and raised in Madisonville, across Lake Pontchartrain, she married Edgar “Dooky” Chase Jr., a jazz trumpeter and bandleader, in 1946, and in time went to work in his parents' restaurant in Tremé, the historic Black neighbourhood beside the French Quarter. She cooked there for some seven decades, into her nineties, and the city called her the Queen of Creole Cuisine. She died in 2019, at ninety-six.

Her story belongs in every Creole lesson because it corrects an old picture. Creole cooking is often told as French cooking carried to New Orleans, but from the start much of it was cooked by Black cooks, enslaved and free, whose names the old cookbooks seldom printed. Chase, a Black woman cooking Creole food for her own community, made plain that it is a Black Creole tradition as much as a French one. Where it came from is told in the roots of Creole cooking.

Her husband's parents opened Dooky Chase's in 1941 as a sandwich shop where neighbours bought po-boys, the city's long sandwiches on French bread, and lottery tickets. From the 1950s she turned it, step by step, into a sit-down restaurant with white tablecloths, a proper dining room and the Creole dishes she cooked.

In the years of segregation, when the law kept Black and white people from dining together, civil rights organisers, Black and white, met and planned over her food, Thurgood Marshall and Martin Luther King Jr. among them. She hung the dining room with art by African American artists, and her own portrait, by Gustave Blache III, hangs in the National Portrait Gallery in Washington.

She cooked for presidents, George W. Bush and Barack Obama among them, and scolded Obama for putting hot sauce in her gumbo before he had tasted it. She is named as an inspiration for Tiana, the young cook of Disney's The Princess and the Frog (2009). After Hurricane Katrina flooded the restaurant in 2005, she and her family rebuilt it.

Two of her dishes are worth a cook's study. Gumbo z'herbes, the green gumbo of many greens, she cooked once a year for Holy Thursday, the day before Good Friday, and the day became a city tradition at her tables. Its method lives in its own entry.

Her fried chicken is the other dish people remember, and a cook learns it by the classic Southern method, done with care. Season the pieces well, dip them in an egg and milk wash, then in seasoned flour, and let them rest a few minutes so the coating sets.

Fry in a deep, heavy pot of oil heated to about 175°C (350°F). The cold chicken drops the oil to around 160 to 165°C (320 to 330°F); hold it there and turn the pieces so the crust browns as the meat cooks through, roughly 12 to 15 minutes for white meat and longer for dark. It is done when the thickest part reaches 74°C (165°F) on a probe. Drain it on a rack, not paper, so the crust stays crisp.

Fried chicken fails in ways a cook learns to read. A dark crust over meat that probes under 74°C (165°F) at the bone means the oil ran too hot: lower the heat and finish the thick pieces on a rack in a 175°C (350°F) oven until they reach temperature. A pale, greasy crust means the oil was too cool or the pot crowded: fry fewer pieces and let the oil recover between batches. Coating that falls away means the chicken went in dripping or was moved too soon: rest the floured pieces and leave them alone until the crust sets.

At the table she is a one-line story: the Queen of Creole Cuisine, who cooked at Dooky Chase's in Tremé for some seven decades and fed civil rights leaders and presidents. Our own gumbo is the Seafood Gumbo; if a guest asks about the green gumbo of Holy Thursday, that is the tradition she kept at Dooky Chase's. Speak of her with the respect the city gives her.
